# Graphing Data

Graphs are fundamental tools for inspecting and communicating with data. 

We begin by importing the `pyplot` plotting library.

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
```
Given data in lists or arrays, we can simply plot that data!
```{python}
x = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
y = [4, 8, 6, 9, 7, 6, 8]
plt.plot(x,y)
plt.show() 
```

## Labels and Limits 

Plotting is not complete unless your plot is properly labeled. A common sequence of commands for plotting with labels may look like this:
```{python}
# Data
year = [1800, 1830, 1880, 1900, 1920, 1990, 2000]
Boston = [24937, 61392, 362839, 560862, 748060, 874283, 589141]
NewYork = [60000, 185000, 1919000, 3802000, 7798000, 16044000, 17800000]

plt.plot(year, Boston, label='Boston') 
plt.plot(year, NewYork, label='New York')

# Display with labels 
plt.xlabel('Year')
plt.ylabel('Population')
plt.title('City Populations')
plt.grid()
plt.legend()
plt.show() 
```

Note that we called `plt.plot()` twice before calling `plt.show()`, which results in the two plots appearing on the same figure. 

## Graph Types

Below are five scenarios that demonstrate five different types of useful Graphs. In addition to the graph, axes are labeled and figures are titled.

### Line Plot {.unnumbered}

The line chart is the default graph type in `pyplot`. Consider the following data representing time and distance traveled during a road trip. 

| $t$   | 0   | 1   | 2    | 3   | 4   | 5   | 6   | 
| :--   | :-- | :-- | :--  | :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- | 
| $d$   | 0   | 42  | 101  | 132 | 138 | 190 | 218 | 
```{python}
t = [ 0,  1,   2,   3,   4,   5,   6]      # Time in hours
d = [ 0, 42, 101, 132, 138, 190, 218]      # Distance in miles 

plt.plot(t,d)

plt.xlabel('Time (hours)')
plt.ylabel('Distance (miles)')
plt.title('Road Trip Progress')
plt.show()
```

### Scatter Plot {.unnumbered}
The following data represents the weight $w$ and price $p$ for a set of cars. 

| $w$   | 2840  | 2900  | 3000  | 2950   | 3150  | 3200  | 3700  | 3900  | 3650  | 3950  |
| :--   | :--   | :--   | :--   | :--    | :--   | :--   | :--   | :--   |  :--  |  :--  |
| $p$   | 22000 | 23500 | 21000 | 21500  | 26000 | 2700  |31000  | 34000 | 39000 | 44000 |

A scatter plot is useful for inspecting and visualizing relationships between variables. 
```{python}
# Weight in pounds, price in dollars
w = [ 2840, 2900, 3000, 2950, 3150, 3200, 3700, 3900, 3650, 3950]
p = [ 22000, 23500, 21000, 21500, 26000, 27000, 31000, 34000, 39000, 44000]

plt.scatter(w,p)

plt.xlabel('Weight (lb)')
plt.ylabel('Price (dollars)')
plt.title('Price per weight of common vehicles')
plt.show() 
```

### Bar Chart {.unnumbered}

A bar chart is useful for comparing different categories. Consider the results of a student survey on study methods:
```{python}
study_methods = ["Flashcards", "ChatBot", "YouTube", "Group Study", "Notes"]
counts = [3, 8, 5, 19, 8]

plt.bar(study_methods, counts)

plt.xlabel("Study Method")
plt.ylabel("Number of Students")
plt.title("Preferred Study Methods")

plt.show()
```

### Histogram {.unnumbered}

A histogram can give you an immediate sense of the distribution of values. Consider the quiz scores in the following example:
```{python}
scores = [ 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, 6, 7, 
           7, 7, 8, 8, 8, 8, 9, 9, 10, 10 ]
           
plt.hist(scores, bins=9, edgecolor='black')

plt.xlabel('Score out of 10')
plt.title('Quiz Score Distribution')
plt.show()
``` 
We used `bins=9` to set the number of histogram bins to 9, and `edgecolor='black'` to help the bins stand out visually. 

We frequently want to compare distributions by plotting them in the same figure. Here is an example with quiz scores from two classes:
```{python}
class_A = [5, 6, 5, 7, 6, 5, 8, 6, 7, 5, 4, 6, 7, 5, 6]
class_B = [9, 8, 10, 9, 10, 8, 9, 10, 6, 8, 9, 7, 8, 10, 9]

plt.hist(class_A, alpha=0.7, bins=9, label='Class A')
plt.hist(class_B, alpha=0.7, bins=9, label='Class B')

plt.legend()
plt.xlabel('Score out of 10')
plt.title('Quiz Score Distributions by Class')
plt.show()
``` 
`alpha=0.7` sets the transparency for each histogram in the figure. An alpha value of 0 would be invisible while 1 would be completely opaque. 

### Box Plot {.unnumbered}

A box plot is a different view of the same type of data we saw with a histogram, and is also useful for comparing distributions. 
```{python}
class_A = [5, 6, 5, 7, 6, 5, 8, 6, 7, 5, 4, 6, 7, 5, 6]
class_B = [9, 8, 10, 9, 10, 8, 9, 10, 6, 8, 9, 7, 8, 10, 9]

plt.boxplot(
    [class_A, class_B],
    labels=["Class A", "Class B"]
)

plt.title('Quiz Score Distributions by Class')
plt.show()
``` 
It is not required that we break up the `boxplot` command onto different lines. It simply helps with readability. Additional categories can be added by extending the lists of data and tick_labels. 

### Plot Summary 

- [**Line Plot**](https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/matplotlib.pyplot.plot.html) -- 
	Shows how a value changes over time or across an ordered sequence. Points are connected with lines to highlight trends. 
- [**Scatter Plot**](https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/matplotlib.pyplot.scatter.html) --
	Displays the relationship between two numerical variables using individual points. It helps reveal patterns, trends, or correlations.
- [**Bar Chart**](https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/matplotlib.pyplot.bar.html) --
	Compares values across categories. The height of each bar represents the size or value of a category.
- [**Histogram**](https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/matplotlib.pyplot.hist.html) --
	Shows the distribution of numerical data by grouping values into bins. It helps to see the overall shape of the distribution and where data are concentrated.
- [**Box Plot**](https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/matplotlib.pyplot.boxplot.html) --
	Summarizes a dataset using the median, quartiles, and possible outliers. It is useful for comparing distributions and understanding spread and variability.

2. Perform a reflex test (or use previous data). Have one person place their hand at the edge of a table with their fingers out. A second person holds a ruler just above the first person's finger tips and lets go at a random time. Without moving their hand, the first person closes their fingers to stop the ruler. For each person,
    - Collect 12 samples of how far the ruler falls before it is caught. 
    - Put the data into a NumPy array. 
	- Create a **histogram** for each person depicting the distribution of their reflex times.
	- Create a **box plot** for each person depicting the distribution of their reflex times.  

3. Consider a pendulum with mass $m$, length $L$, and release angle $\theta$. The **period** $T$ of a pendulum is the amount of time it takes to complete one cycle of motion, swinging from one side to the other and then back again. To model the period of a pendulum, we want to determine the effect that each of the variables $m$, $L$, and $\theta$ have on $T$. We can explore this experimentally by keeping two of the variables constant while changing the third and looking for changes in $T$.
